name: Sun Yat-sen
info: Sun Yat-sen (1866-1925) was a Chinese physician and revolutionary who led anti-Qing movements from exile, became first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912 and founded the Kuomintang's political creed, the Three Principles of the People.

facts.born: 12 November 1866 in the village of Cuiheng, Xiangshan County (now Zhongshan), Guangdong; son of Sun Dacheng, a poor farmer, tailor and porter, and Madame Yang; Hakka and Cantonese
facts.died: 12 March 1925 in Beijing, aged 58, of cancer; long reported as liver cancer, the autopsy found a gallbladder cancer that had spread to the liver
facts.role: Physician, licensed 1892; founder of the Revive China Society (1894) and leader of the Tongmenghui (1905); provisional president of the Republic of China, 1912; leader of the Kuomintang; head of the military government in Guangzhou from 1921
facts.known: the 1911 Revolution; first provisional president of the Republic of China; founding the Kuomintang; the Three Principles of the People; the First United Front with the Soviet Union and the Chinese Communist Party; the Whampoa Military Academy

t: After Li Hongzhang ignored his reform petition in 1894, Sun spent most of seventeen years in exile raising money among overseas Chinese for a series of failed uprisings against the Qing.
When the Wuchang uprising of 1911 brought down the dynasty, he was elected provisional president but gave the office to Yuan Shikai in 1912 in return for the emperor's abdication.
Fighting Yuan and the warlords from a base in Guangzhou, he allied with the Soviet Union and the Chinese Communist Party, and both the Republic of China and the People's Republic now claim him.
dyk: Sun's best-known name in Chinese, Sun Zhongshan, comes from Nakayama, the Japanese pseudonym Tōten Miyazaki gave him while he hid in Japan; his birthplace was renamed Zhongshan after his death.
ev: Sun graduates from the Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese
His petition to Li Hongzhang is ignored and he founds the Revive China Society in Hawaii
The First Guangzhou Uprising fails and Sun goes into exile
He forms the Tongmenghui with Chinese students in Tokyo
Sun takes office as provisional president, then resigns in favour of Yuan Shikai
The Second Revolution against Yuan fails and Sun flees to Japan
The Sun-Joffe Manifesto opens his alliance with the Soviet Union
Sun dies of cancer in Beijing

sections.early:
Sun Yat-sen, whose genealogical name was Sun Deming, was born on 12 November 1866 in Cuiheng, Xiangshan County, Guangdong, to Sun Dacheng and Madame Yang. His father owned very little land and worked as a tailor in Macau, a journeyman and a porter. He began school at ten, and in 1878, aged 13, went to live with his elder brother Sun Mei in Honolulu in the Kingdom of Hawaii. Sun Mei paid for him at the ʻIolani School, where he learned English, British history, mathematics, science and Christianity and received a prize from King Kalākaua before graduating in 1882. He learned American history and admired Abraham Lincoln and Alexander Hamilton, and he took Hawaii's economic development as a model.

Worried by his brother's growing Christianity, Sun Mei sent him home in 1883. In Cuiheng Sun and his friend Lu Haodong broke the wooden idol of the North Star God, and his parents sent him to Hong Kong, where he studied at the Diocesan Home and the Government Central School and was baptised by the American missionary Charles Robert Hager in 1884. He studied medicine in Guangzhou under John Glasgow Kerr and at the Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese, graduating in 1892 as one of two of a class of twelve.
sections.rise:
In Hong Kong Sun belonged to a circle of revolutionaries nicknamed the Four Bandits and met Yeung Ku-wan of the Furen Literary Society. In 1894 he wrote an 8,000-character petition to the Qing viceroy Li Hongzhang on modernising China and went to Tianjin to present it, but was not received; he then turned irrevocably to revolution. That year he founded the Revive China Society in Hawaii, the first Chinese nationalist revolutionary society, whose members swore to "Expel the Tartar barbarians, restore China." After China's defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War, he and Zou Rong sought a republic, while Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao favoured reform under the dynasty.

The First Guangzhou Uprising of 26 October 1895 was betrayed and more than 70 members, including Lu Haodong, were captured. In exile, Sun was detained at the Chinese Legation in London in October 1896 and freed after 12 days through James Cantlie, the press and the Foreign Office, which made him a hero in Britain. From 1897 he lived in Japan with the support of Tōten Miyazaki, Tōyama Mitsuru and Inukai Tsuyoshi, helped the Filipino diplomat Mariano Ponce ship arms to the Philippines, and raised money in Bangkok, the United States, Singapore and Malaya, calling overseas Chinese "the Mother of the Revolution".
sections.deeds:
On 20 August 1905 Sun joined Chinese students in Tokyo to form the Tongmenghui, with the aims of expelling the Manchu, reviving China, founding a republic and distributing land equally; his Three Principles of the People were nationalism, democracy and the people's welfare. Uprisings it sponsored in 1907 and 1908 failed, and the Yellow Flower Mound Uprising of 27 April 1911, led by Huang Xing, ended in disaster. On 10 October 1911 the Wuchang uprising began the Xinhai Revolution. Sun, in the United States, read of it in the press and reached China on 21 December 1911.

On 29 December provincial representatives at Nanjing elected him provisional president, as some argued a compromise between Li Yuanhong and Huang Xing; the new republic dated its calendar from 1 January 1912. Yuan Shikai of the Beiyang Army had been promised the presidency if the Qing abdicated, and when the emperor did so on 12 February 1912 Sun stepped down. After the Kuomintang won the 1912-1913 elections, its leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated, almost certainly on Yuan's secret order, and Sun's Second Revolution of 1913 failed. From 1921 he headed a military government in Guangzhou, and with Soviet help he founded the Whampoa Military Academy under Chiang Kai-shek in the First United Front with the Communists.
sections.opponents:
Sun's opponents were the Qing court, then Yuan Shikai, who banned the Kuomintang and in 1915 proclaimed himself emperor, and the warlords of the north. Within the Tongmenghui, after repeated failures, Tao Chengzhang and Zhang Binglin published a leaflet denouncing his "criminal acts" and accusing him of leading revolts for profit; the movement split into pro-Sun and anti-Sun camps, and in 1910 its headquarters moved from Singapore to Penang. In Guangzhou he faced Chen Jiongming's revolt and the uprising of the Canton Merchant Volunteers Corps.

His methods and views have drawn criticism. He used the triads to raise money and supported bandit leaders such as Bai Lang. Some historians allege he was not a real Christian, since he seldom went to church. He was highly critical of Chinese traditions that did not meet Western standards, breaking idols and denouncing Chinese medicine. He supported natalism and eugenics, favouring the sterilisation of those perceived as unfit and opposing birth control. In 1902, already married in China, he married the Japanese teenager Kaoru Otsuki, and he kept Asada Haru as a mistress. He praised Lenin as a "great man", and Lenin praised the Kuomintang.
sections.last:
In 1923 Sun broadcast a Peaceful Reunification Manifesto asking the warlords to reduce their troops, signed the Sun-Joffe Manifesto with the Soviet envoy Adolph Joffe and accepted the adviser Mikhail Borodin, whom he called his "Lafayette". In 1924 he had his brother-in-law T. V. Soong found the Canton Central Bank. That November he went north to Tianjin and Beijing to call for a national conference, an end to warlord rule and the abolition of the unequal treaties, and at Kobe later that month he spoke on Pan-Asianism, contrasting the "kingly way" of the East with the "hegemonic way" of the West.

An exploratory operation at Peking Union Medical College Hospital on 26 January 1925 found cancer, and Sun was treated with radium and then, against his doctors' advice, with traditional Chinese medicine. He died in Beijing on 12 March 1925, aged 58. He left three testaments, to the party and his family, both drafted by Wang Jingwei, and one he dictated to the Soviet Union hailing it as the bulwark of anti-imperialism. His body was embalmed and kept at the Temple of Azure Clouds outside Beijing, and on 1 June 1929 it was moved to the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum on Purple Mountain in Nanjing.
sections.legacy:
After Sun's death Wang Jingwei led the Nationalist government, which split into rival factions, each claiming his ambiguous legacy. Chiang Kai-shek married Soong Mei-ling, sister of Sun's widow Soong Ching-ling, and after the Shanghai massacre of 1927 the Nationalists and Communists, then at civil war, both claimed to be his true heirs. A personality cult grew round Sun and Chiang in the Republic of China; the Kuomintang keeps him as its president in its constitution, and Caodaism in Vietnam worships him. In 1940 the government named him Father of the Nation, a title that after 1949 continued only in Taiwan, where in 2004 a proposal of the Ministry of Education to call him a foreigner rather than Taiwan's father met angry protest.

In the People's Republic he is honoured as the Forerunner of the Revolution and named in the preamble to the constitution. Mao Zedong's essay On New Democracy of 1940 recast his doctrine as the New Three Principles of the People, a reading that his granddaughter Lily Sun said distorted his legacy. He remains unique among 20th-century Chinese leaders for having a high reputation in both Mainland China and Taiwan, and his portrait appears in Tiananmen Square on May Day and National Day.

summary: Sun Yat-sen, a doctor educated in Hawaii and Hong Kong, spent years in exile raising money for uprisings against the Qing, was elected provisional president of the new Republic of China in 1912 and soon yielded to Yuan Shikai. He then fought the warlords from Guangzhou with Soviet and Communist help and died in 1925, leaving a legacy claimed by both the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party.
references: Marie-Claire Bergère, Sun Yat-sen (Stanford University Press, 2000)
notes: The article dates the Kobe Pan-Asianism speech to 28 November 1924 in one place and 29 November in another; the section says 'at Kobe on 28 November', which the editor may want to make 'in late November'.
The article contradicts itself on the 1900 return to Japan versus his 1897 arrival; I kept 1897.
Wives: the article names his first wife only as 'a wife in China'; I did not name her.
